correctness.rationale: The target is equivalently B^n<A^(n+1), with A=pi(n^2) and B=A+d. For n>=1000, explicit Brun--Titchmarsh bounds d from above and Rosser--Schoenfeld bounds A from below. After log(1+u)<u, the left side is below 8+4/n<9, while the lower bound A>50000 gives log A>9. The exact packaged sieve exhaustively checks every n from 3 through 999 with arbitrary-precision integer powers, so no finite or infinite case is omitted.

evidence: Conjecture 2.7(i) compares pi(kn)^(1/k) with pi((k+1)n)^(1/(k+1)) at fixed scale n.
With k=n it reaches n(n+1) on the right, which is below (n+1)^2; with scale n+1 it starts at n(n+1), which is above n^2.
Therefore either substitution weakens the wrong side and does not imply the square-endpoint inequality.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The implication comparison is endpoint-sensitive, not title-based. The previous fixed-scale statement and the present square-scale statement are logically distinct, and monotonicity of pi is insufficient to bridge either mismatch in the needed direction.

value.rationale: The theorem resolves an explicit conjecture from a paper devoted to sixty open problems on exact prime-counting behavior. It replaces numerical evidence by a complete proof for all n>=3, with a transparent mechanism linking the local count of primes between consecutive squares to the accumulated value pi(n^2). The finite computation has a bounded supporting role and the mathematical content is the uniform analytic tail.
